etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English frank, from Old French franc (“free”), in turn from the name of an early Germanic confederation, the Franks, from Proto-West Germanic *frankō (“javelin, spear”). Doublet of Frank, franc, and farang.

definitions.definition: Honest, especially in a manner that seems slightly blunt; candid; not reserved or disguised.
(obsolete) Unbounded by restrictions, limitations, etc.; free.

quote.citation: 1591, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “Prosopopoia. Or Mother Hubberds Tale.”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. […], London:  […]  William Ponsonbie, […], →OCLC:

1692, Roger L’Estrange, “ (please specify the fable number.) (please specify the name of the fable.)”, in Fables, of Æsop and Other Eminent Mythologists: […], London:  […]  R[ichard] Sare, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Frank of Civilities that cost them nothing.

quote.citation: 1591, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “Muiopotmos, or The Fate of the Butterflie”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. […], London:  […]  William Ponsonbie, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Over the fields, in his franke lustinesse, And all the champain o're he soared light.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Free postage, a right exercised by governments (usually with definite article).

quote.citation: October 5, 1780, William Cowper, letter to Rev. William Unwin
quote.text: I have said so much, that, if I had not a frank, I must burn my letter and begin again.

definitions.definition: (countable) The notice on an envelope where a stamp would normally be found.

quote.citation: 1842, [anonymous collaborator of Letitia Elizabeth Landon], “(please specify the page)”, in Lady Anne Granard; or, Keeping up Appearances. […], volume II, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, pages 178–179:
quote.text: But, although her friends were kind, Lady Anne was not easy; neither daughter made her appearance, nor did she receive a letter to account for their silence. She remembered, indeed, that Charles Penrhyn could not get franks now, and her daughters knew she would not pay postage; and she had commanded Helen to work night and day, saying, "surely they can give her common materials."

definitions.definition: (transitive) To place a frank on an envelope.

quote.citation: 1811, [Jane Austen], chapter 20, in Sense and Sensibility […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  C[harles] Roworth, […], and published by T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: It will be so ridiculous to see all his letters directed to him with an M.P.—But do you know, he says, he will never frank for me?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To exempt from charge for postage, as a letter, package, or packet, etc.
(transitive) To send by public conveyance free of expense.

quote.text: This required extensive correspondence; so, in the next place, the privilege of franking letters in reference to the emigrants' registration office, was obtained—much to the indignation of red tapists.

quote.citation: 1957, Jack Kerouac, chapter 1, in On the Road, Viking Press, →OCLC, part 1:
quote.text: We had a farewell meal of franks and beans in a Seventh Avenue Riker’s, and then Dean got on the bus that said Chicago and roared off into the night.

quote.citation: 1978, Superman: The Movie, spoken by Perry White (Jackie Cooper):
quote.text: I want the name of this flying whatchamacallit to go with the Daily Planet like bacon and eggs, franks and beans, death and taxes, politics and corruption!

quote.citation: 1988 June 28, “Cold Lampin' With Flavor” (track 4), in It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back‎[1], performed by Public Enemy:
quote.text: I'm in my Flavmobile cold lamping. I took a G upstate cold camping. To the Poconos, we call a hideaways. A bag of franks and a bag of Frito-Lays.

definitions.definition: To shut up in a frank or sty; to pen up; hence, to cram; to fatten.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Marry, as for Clarence, he is well repaid; He is franked up to fatting for his pains

definitions.definition: (historical) Obsolete form of franc, former French coins, moneys of account, and currency.

quote.citation: 1771, Encyclopaedia Britannica, 1st ed., Vol. II, p. 630:
quote.text: Frank, or Franc, an ancient coin, either of gold or ſilver, ſtruck and current in France. The value of the gold frank was ſomewhat more than that of the gold crown; the ſilver frank was a third of the gold one; this coin is long out of uſe, though the term is ſtill retained as the name of a money of account; in which ſenſe it is equivalent to the livre, or twenty ſols.
